html:
The Quechua are the Indigenous peoples of the Andes who speak Quechua, the largest family of Native American languages, with several million speakers in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador and nearby countries. The map spreads this label along the Andes in 1492.

Quechua probably began on the central coast or highlands of Peru many centuries before the Incas. The Inca Empire made a form of it, runa simi, "people's speech", its language of government, and spread it along the Inca roads by moving whole communities. That is why Quechua is now spoken from southern Colombia to northern Argentina.

The Spanish kept using it to rule and to preach. The Doctrina Christiana of 1584, the first book printed in South America, was in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara. Quechua people led great revolts, above all that of Túpac Amaru II in 1780.

Today most Quechua speakers are farmers or city people of the Andes. Peru and Bolivia recognise Quechua as an official language, but many young people switch to Spanish. Regional forms include the Kichwa of Ecuador and the Kichwa Lamista of the Amazon edge.
